claims.source: To ensure that metabolic or imaging artifacts did not drive the observation of these stochastic population cortical responses, local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded in the AC while simultaneously conducting FA imaging, and the LFPs also showed all-or-none response patterns that strongly correlated with the FA signals (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous LFP recording and FA imaging (Figure 2F).

claims.claim: Stochastic population AC responses were observed in brain slices prepared using a different anesthetic (isoflurane) without transcardiac perfusion in a different laboratory using a biphasic stimulator vs. monophasic stimulator.
claims.source: We also observed stochastic population AC responses in brain slices prepared using a different anesthetic (isoflurane) without transcardiac perfusion in a different laboratory using a biphasic stimulator vs. monophasic stimulator (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the stochastic responses were not specific to a particular slice preparation or stimulation technique.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a different laboratory setup (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and inference about the generalizability of the findings.

claims.claim: Stimulus-evoked calcium signals of a small population of layer 4 cells showed that a similar population of layer 4 cells was activated with each population ON response and that population OFF responses were associated with an absence of layer four responses.
claims.source: Looking more closely at the activity of cortical layer 4 cells, the stimulus-evoked calcium signals of a small population of layer 4 cells following IC stimulation showed that a similar population layer 4 cells was activated with each population ON response and that population OFF responses were associated with an absence of layer four responses. For instance, all neurons ceased to respond during stimuli # 9 and 11 (Figure 2G, rose ribbons, Figure 2—source data 4) and (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging of layer 4 cells (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claims.claim: Whole-cell recordings of layer 4 cells during population ON responses revealed a plateau of depolarization upon which rode several action potentials, resembling previously described UP states.
claims.source: Whole-cell recordings of layer 4 cells during population ON population responses revealed a plateau of depolarization upon which rode several action potentials (Figure 2H, green box, Figure 2—source data 5), resembling previously described UP states (Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Rigas and Castro-Alamancos, 2007; Fanselow and Connors, 2010), which was supported by the bimodal distribution shown by the post stimulus membrane potential of such layer 4 cells during population ON cortical responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 1, see, Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and citations to previous studies describing UP states.

claims.claim: IC stimulation produces stochastic population responses in the AC, and these population responses are stereotyped and represent stimulus-induced UP states.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that IC stimulation produces stochastic population responses in the AC, and that these population responses are stereotyped and represent stimulus-induced UP states.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Population ON/OFF cortical responses occurred only after electrical stimulation of IC, and not by the direct stimulation of MGB or the subcortical white matter.
claims.source: Population ON/OFF cortical responses occurred only after electrical stimulation of IC, and not by the direct stimulation of MGB or the subcortical white matter (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2, Kruskal-Wallis: p=0.001, pairwise comparison: p=0.023 for IC vs. MGB or subcortical white matter and p=1 for MGB vs. subcortical white matter, Dunn's post hoc test, n = 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing stimulation at different sites (Figure 3B, 3D) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The percentage of population ON cortical responses increased with increasing amplitude of the stimulating current.
claims.source: Similar to the in vivo data, the percentage of population ON cortical responses increased with increasing amplitude of the stimulating current (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 4, RM-ANOVA: *F(3,9)=9.7, p=0.003, pairwise comparison: *p=0.009 for 50 vs. 150–200 μA, *p=0.008 for 50 vs. 250–300 μA, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 4 slices from four animals), which was consistent with the in vivo results (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between stimulating current amplitude and response frequency (Figure 3E) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: There was a log-linear relationship between the FA signals of either IC or MGB and the stimulating current amplitude.
claims.source: Moreover, while there was a log-linear relationship between the FA signals of either IC or MGB and the stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 5, R2 = 0.68, p=2.2×10−19 for IC and R2 = 0.53, p=3.3×10−13 for MGB), this relationship was lost between the cortical responses and stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 5, R2 = 0.004, p=0.6), suggesting that the magnitude of the cortical response is not predictable from stimulus amplitude.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between FA signals and stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F) and statistical analysis, with inference about predictability.

claims.claim: Bath application of gabazine (SR-95531, 200 nM), the GABAΑ-R blocker, was able to retrieve all missing cortical responses compared to control.
claims.source: Under simultaneous FA imaging and IC stimulation, gabazine perfusion was able to retrieve all missing cortical responses compared to control (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2, Kruskal-Wallis: p=2.5×10−7, pairwise comparison: p=5.08×10−4 for gabazine vs. control, p=4.1×10−7 for gabazine vs. wash, and p=0.34 for control vs. wash, Dunn's post hoc test, n = 14 trials obtained from five animals), which suggested that the population OFF cortical responses were driven by inhibitory inputs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4B, 4C) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Layer 4 cells demonstrated a surge of evoked post-stimulus IPSCs during population ON cortical responses only.
claims.source: Consistent with the previous finding that stimulation of the IC evoked a post-stimulus UP-states activity in layer 4 cells during the population ON cortical responses only (Figure 2H; Fanselow and Connors, 2010; Haider et al., 2006), layer 4 cells demonstrated a surge of evoked post-stimulus IPSCs during population ON cortical responses only (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4D) and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MGB cells showed evoked post-stimulus IPSCs following every trial of IC stimulation during population ON and population OFF cortical responses.
claims.source: In contrast, MGB cells showed evoked post-stimulus IPSCs following every trial of IC stimulation during population ON and population OFF cortical responses (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: Evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCs in layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses.
claims.source: Quantitatively, while these evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCS in the layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 3, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test: p=0.006 for IPSCs, n = 10 cells from four animals and p=0.036 for EPSCs, n = 6 cells from four animals), the evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 4, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.011 for IPSCs, n = 20 cells from seven animals and p=0.56 for EPSCs, n = 14 cells from four animals).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4F, 4G) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges.
claims.source: Quantitatively, while these evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCS in the layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 3, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test: p=0.006 for IPSCs, n = 10 cells from four animals and p=0.036 for EPSCs, n = 6 cells from four animals), the evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 4, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.011 for IPSCs, n = 20 cells from seven animals and p=0.56 for EPSCs, n = 14 cells from four animals).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4G) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: MGB cells receive more inhibition during population OFF cortical responses with no change in excitation.
claims.source: These findings suggest that MGB cells receive more inhibition during population OFF cortical responses with no change in excitation, which led us to hypothesize that MGB activity could be modulated by inhibitory inputs during the population OFF cortical responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Specific injection of gabazine into the MGB in the aCTC slice was able to significantly increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses.
claims.source: Under simultaneous FA imaging and IC stimulation, the specific injection of gabazine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) into the MGB in the aCTC slice was able to significantly increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses (Figure 4I and J, Figure 4—source data 5 and 6), indicated by the Δf/f of the evoked cortical FA signals (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 7, RM-ANOVA: F(3,21) = 13.9, p=3.17×10−5, pairwise comparison: *p=5.9×10−5, 1.5 × 10−4, 0.0026 for gabazine in MGB vs. control, wash, and gabazine in AC, respectively, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 8 slices from seven animals).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4I, 4J, 4K) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Selective gabazine injection into the AC did not increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses.
claims.source: In contrast, the same effect was not observed after selective gabazine injection into the AC (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 7, RM-ANOVA: F(3,21) = 13.9, pairwise comparison: p=0.73 and 1.0 for gabazine in AC vs. control and wash, respectively, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 8 slices from seven animals), consistent with data obtained from the whole-cell recording of layer 4 cells (Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4K) and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Population OFF cortical responses could be driven by thalamic inhibition.

claims.claim: The mean peak latencies of IPSCs and EPSCs received by MGB cells showed no difference during population ON and population OFF cortical responses.

results.result: In vivo transcranial calcium imaging of anesthetized GCaMP6s mice revealed stochastic all-or-none population responses in the primary auditory cortex (A1) following repeated presentations of pure tones. These population ON and OFF responses were independent of stimulus presentation order, formed two distinct classes in histogram analysis, and increased in frequency with increasing sound pressure level.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from in vivo calcium imaging (Figures 1A-F) demonstrating stochastic cortical responses. The experimental design is appropriate, data show clear bimodal response patterns, and the relationship between stimulus intensity and response probability is well-documented with statistical support.

results.result: In vitro electrical stimulation of the inferior colliculus (IC) in auditory colliculo-thalamocortical (aCTC) brain slices recapitulated the stochastic cortical responses observed in vivo. While IC, MGB, and TRN showed consistent responses to each stimulus, the auditory cortex exhibited all-or-none population responses that were validated by simultaneous LFP recordings and replicated across different experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C11-C12 demonstrate robust replication of the in vivo phenomenon in brain slices using multiple recording modalities (FA imaging, calcium imaging, whole-cell recording, LFP). The consistency across different laboratories and preparation methods (C12) strengthens the validity of the findings.

results.result: Population ON cortical responses involve stereotyped activation of layer 4 cells that exhibit UP state-like depolarization plateaus with action potentials, while population OFF responses are associated with absence of layer 4 activity. These responses represent stimulus-induced UP states in the auditory cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 are supported by calcium imaging and whole-cell recordings from layer 4 cells (Figures 2G-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 6). The bimodal membrane potential distribution and resemblance to previously described UP states provide strong evidence for the characterization of these responses.

results.result: Stochastic population ON/OFF cortical responses occurred only after electrical stimulation of the IC, not after direct stimulation of MGB or subcortical white matter. The percentage of population ON responses increased with stimulating current amplitude, but the magnitude of cortical responses was not predictable from stimulus amplitude despite log-linear relationships between stimulus amplitude and IC or MGB activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are well-supported by systematic comparison of stimulation sites (Figure 3B, 3D) and current amplitudes (Figure 3E-F) with appropriate statistical analyses. The loss of linear relationship at the cortical level (R²=0.004, p=0.6) is a key finding demonstrating the gating nature of the phenomenon.

results.result: Population OFF cortical responses are driven by thalamic inhibition. Bath application of gabazine retrieved all missing cortical responses. Layer 4 cells showed reduced IPSCs and EPSCs during population OFF responses, while MGB cells showed larger IPSCs during population OFF responses with no change in EPSCs. Specific gabazine injection into MGB, but not AC, significantly increased population ON responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C27 provide comprehensive pharmacological and electrophysiological evidence (Figure 4) demonstrating that thalamic inhibition drives population OFF responses. The specificity of the MGB effect (C25-C26) and the differential synaptic changes in layer 4 vs. MGB cells (C22-C23) are well-documented with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Population ON responses are associated with synchronized MGB cell activity. While mean peak latencies of IPSCs and EPSCs in MGB cells showed no difference between population ON and OFF responses, approximately 50% of MGB cells received earlier IPSCs during population OFF responses. The variance of peak latencies of evoked calcium signals from thalamic cells was significantly larger during population OFF responses, suggesting that synchronous thalamic relay cell activity is required for population ON responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by whole-cell recordings and calcium imaging data (Figure 5A-F) with appropriate statistical analyses. The increased variance in thalamic response timing during population OFF responses (p=0.033) provides mechanistic insight into how desynchronization prevents cortical activation.

results.result: Population OFF cortical responses are driven by feedback inhibition of MGB through the corticothalamic layer 6-TRN pathway. Photoinhibition or chemogenetic inhibition of layer 6 corticothalamic cells significantly increased population ON responses, while inhibition of layer 5 cells or IC GABAergic cells had no effect. Blocking TRN activity with NBQX also increased population ON responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 provide strong converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (optogenetics, chemogenetics, pharmacology) with appropriate controls (C33, C35, C37, C38) demonstrating the specific role of the layer 6-TRN pathway. Statistical support is robust across all manipulations (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

results.result: FA and calcium signals from the MGB are smaller than those from AC, possibly due to limited alignment of mitochondria-containing neuropil processes or low baseline expression of GCaMP in the MGB.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is supported by citations to previous studies (Dana et al., 2014; Llano et al., 2009) and is consistent with known technical limitations of these imaging approaches in thalamic structures. The proposed mechanisms are reasonable inferences.

results.result: Stochastic population cortical responses were observed in the mouse AC both in vivo and in vitro. Population ON responses were associated with synchronized MGB cell responses, while population OFF responses were associated with TRN-mediated inhibition of MGB under control of layer 6 corticothalamic projections. Inhibitory projections from IC to MGB had no impact on population ON response probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 represent summary statements of the major findings that are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript (Figures 1-6). These conclusions logically follow from the experimental evidence.

results.result: Population OFF cortical responses are unlikely to represent cortical adaptation because they show all-or-none characteristics rather than gradual amplitude decreases. Layer 6 corticothalamic neurons gate population activity in the AC via their projections to TRN, which desynchronize MGB neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are reasonable inferences based on the experimental data and comparison to adaptation literature. The all-or-none nature of responses (documented in Figures 1-2) is inconsistent with typical adaptation patterns, and the gating mechanism is well-supported by the layer 6 manipulation experiments (Figure 6).

results.result: The gating mechanism involves TRN-based desynchronization of thalamocortical neurons rather than diminishing overall thalamic response. This is consistent with the finding that direct electrical stimulation of the thalamus did not lead to stochastic AC responses because it likely elicits highly synchronous MGB responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are well-supported inferences from the experimental data (Figures 3, 5) and are consistent with previous work on TRN function (Pita-Almenar et al., 2014). The mechanistic explanation is logical and supported by the timing and synchrony data.

results.result: Population OFF cortical responses were never initiated by the first IC stimulation but only by subsequent stimulations, suggesting they require prior cortical activity. The high probability of OFF responses at low stimulation levels suggests cortico-reticulothalamic control is most effective when signal-to-noise ratio is low, consistent with the notion that top-down modulation is required for attentional modulation of weak signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by observations from the stimulation experiments (Figures 1F, 3E) and represent reasonable inferences about the functional significance of the findings. The relationship between stimulus intensity and OFF response probability is well-documented.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within existing literature on stochastic cortical responses, corticothalamic control, classical vs. alternative models of sensory processing, TRN function, and potential relevance to schizophrenia.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C46, C53-C54, C58-C59, C61 accurately represent prior work through appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The manuscript discusses alternative mechanisms and broader implications, including possible intracortical effects of layer 6 manipulation, the potential role of thalamocortical transmission in selecting cortical ensembles, and predictions about consequences of TRN disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C55-C56, C60 represent speculative statements about alternative mechanisms and broader implications. While these are reasonable hypotheses, they are explicitly acknowledged as speculation and would require additional experiments to validate. The authors appropriately identify these as areas for future work.

results.result: The data suggest that at the thalamocortical level, sensory inputs activate stereotyped patterns of population cortical activity, with the thalamus recruiting cortical ensembles of pre-wired sensory representations in conjunction with internal cortical dynamics. Corticothalamic modulators control temporal coordination between thalamic cells to gate activation of intracortical networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C62-C63 represent the major conceptual conclusions of the manuscript. These inferences are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data demonstrating stereotyped cortical responses (Figures 1-2), the role of thalamic synchrony (Figure 5), and corticothalamic gating (Figure 6).
